title: Hands-on Exercise 1b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Thematic mapping uses map symbols to visualise selected properties of geographic features that are not naturally visible, such as population, temperature, crime rate, and property prices.
Geovisualisation combines cartography, computer science, and information visualisation to explore, analyse, and communicate geospatial data, enhancing spatial understanding and knowledge discovery.
In this hands-on exercise, I learn how to plot functional and truthful choropleth maps using the tmap package in R.

text:
Getting Started
The following R packages are used in this exercise:

tmap — for thematic map creation
sf — for handling geospatial data
tidyverse (includes readr, tidyr, dplyr) — for data import and wrangling


pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R

Importing Data into R

The Data
Two datasets are used:

Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) (GeoJSON) from data.gov.sg — geospatial data providing Singapore’s planning subzone boundaries based on URA Master Plan 2019.
Singapore Residents by Planning Area / Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling, June 2024 (respopagesextod2024.csv) from Department of Statistics, Singapore — aspatial data with PA and SZ fields used to georeference to the subzone boundaries.



Importing Geospatial Data into R
st_read() is used to import the GeoJSON file, and the data is immediately transformed to the SVY21 projected coordinate system (EPSG: 3414). Unlike KML, the GeoJSON format already encodes attribute fields as proper columns, so no additional parsing is needed.

mpsz <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson") %>%

Importing Attribute Data into R
The population CSV file is imported using read_csv():

popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv")



Data Preparation
A data table with 2024 values is prepared with the variables: PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, and DEPENDENCY.

YOUNG: age groups 0–4 to 20–24
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age groups 25–29 to 60–64
AGED: age group 65 and above
TOTAL: all age groups
DEPENDENCY: ratio of (YOUNG + AGED) to ECONOMY ACTIVE


Data wrangling
pivot_wider() from tidyr and mutate(), filter(), group_by(), select() from dplyr are used. Column names are referenced explicitly in rowSums() instead of positional indices, as pivot_wider() sorts age group columns alphabetically (causing 5_to_9 to appear after 55_to_59), which makes positional indexing unreliable:

popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG,
              values_from = POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(select(., `0_to_4`, `5_to_9`, `10_to_14`,
                                   `15_to_19`, `20_to_24`),
                         na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(select(., `25_to_29`, `30_to_34`,
                                              `35_to_39`, `40_to_44`,
                                              `45_to_49`, `50_to_54`,
                                              `55_to_59`, `60_to_64`),
                                    na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(`AGED` = rowSums(select(., `65_to_69`, `70_to_74`, `75_to_79`,
                                    `80_to_84`, `85_to_89`, `90_and_over`),
                          na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(`TOTAL` = rowSums(select(., `0_to_4`:`90_and_over`),
                           na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)



Joining attribute data and geospatial data
The PA and SZ values are converted to uppercase to match SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N, and rows with no economy active population are removed:

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ),
            .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

left_join() joins the geospatial and attribute data using SUBZONE_N and SZ as the common identifier. Using mpsz as the left table ensures the output remains a simple feature data frame:

mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2024,
                           by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))

Saving the joined data frame as an RDS file for future use:

dir.create("data/rds/", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Choropleth Mapping with tmap
Two approaches are available for creating choropleth maps in tmap:

Quick plot using qtm()
Fully customisable map using tmap layer elements


Quick choropleth map with qtm()
qtm() provides a concise way to produce a standard choropleth map. tmap_mode("plot") sets the output to a static map:

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024,
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")










Customisable choropleth map using tmap elements
For finer control over cartographic quality, tmap’s individual drawing elements are used:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))









Drawing a base map
tm_shape() defines the input data, and tm_polygons() draws the polygon layer with default styling (light gray fill, dark gray borders):

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()










Choropleth map using tm_polygons()
Assigning a variable to fill within tm_polygons() produces a choropleth map. The default classification method is pretty and the default colour scheme is blues3:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")










Using tm_fill() and tm_borders()
tm_polygons() is a wrapper of tm_fill() and tm_borders(). Using them separately provides more control. tm_fill() alone (no borders):

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")








Adding borders with tm_borders():

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()








Customising border appearance with col, lwd, and lty:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")











Data Classification Methods
tmap supports ten classification methods: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks. The style argument in tm_scale_intervals() is used to specify the method.

Quantile classification (5 classes)

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










Equal interval classification (5 classes)

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








The quantile method produces more evenly distributed class sizes compared to equal interval, which can be skewed by data distribution.


Custom break points
Descriptive statistics are checked first to inform break point choices:

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.0000  0.6750  0.7283  0.7563  0.8140 10.0000      94 


Custom breaks are set at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90, with minimum 0 and maximum 1.00:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











Colour Scheme

Using ColourBrewer palette
The values argument in tm_scale_intervals() accepts ColourBrewer palette names:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








To reverse the colour direction, prefix the palette name with -:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










Cartographic furniture
tm_compass(), tm_scalebar(), tm_grid(), and tm_credits() add map furniture:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))











Map Layout

Map legend
fill.legend and tm_legend() customise the legend position and title:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_pos_auto_in() +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))










Map style
tmap_style() applies predefined layout themes. The natural style is used below:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")








Resetting to the default white style:

tmap_style("white")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Small multiple maps (facet maps) place many maps side-by-side to show how spatial patterns change with respect to another variable. In tmap, they can be created three ways.

By assigning multiple values to an aesthetic argument
Assigning two variables to fill generates side-by-side choropleth maps:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal",
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")










By arranging maps in a grid layout with tmap_arrange()
Individual maps are created separately and then arranged:

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of young population")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of aged population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp = 1, ncol = 2)










By defining a group-by variable in tm_facets()
tm_facets() splits the map by a categorical variable:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2,
            ncol = 3,
            free.coords = TRUE,
            drop.units = TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = TRUE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"),
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

section: Complementing Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
text:
Complementing Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
Maps and statistical charts complement each other — maps show spatial patterns while charts display numerical distributions. tmap supports embedding statistical charts directly into map visualisations using the fill.chart argument.
Adding a box plot to the Central Region dependency map:

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)








Outliers in the dependency distribution are highlighted on the choropleth map using red borders and subzone labels:

mpsz_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

stats <- boxplot.stats(mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- mpsz_selected[mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tm_shape(mpsz_selected) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_text("SUBZONE_N", col = "red", size = 0.7) +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1b: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
Creating Interactive Maps
tmap_mode("view") switches to interactive mode, allowing users to zoom, pan, and click on features for popup information.
Basic interactive map of the Central Region:

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected,
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name"       = "SUBZONE_N",
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2)





tmap_mode("plot")

To prevent users from zooming too far out of the study area, set_zoom_limits restricts the zoom range:

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected,
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name"       = "SUBZONE_N",
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(12, 14))





tmap_mode("plot")

Setting set_zoom_limits = c(12, 14) restricts how far users can zoom in (level 14) and out (level 12), keeping the focus on the Central Region throughout exploration.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Data Acquisition
The following datasets are used in this exercise:

Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) from data.gov.sg
Pre-Schools Location from data.gov.sg
Cycling Path from LTADataMall
Singapore Airbnb listing data from Inside Airbnb

The geospatial files (MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL, CyclingPathGazette, and PreSchoolsLocation.kml) are placed in the data/geospatial sub-folder. The aspatial file listings.csv is placed in the data/aspatial sub-folder.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Getting Started
Two R packages are used in this exercise:

sf — for importing, managing, and processing geospatial data
tidyverse — for data science tasks including importing, wrangling, and visualising data

Within tidyverse, the following packages are specifically used: readr (importing csv), tidyr (manipulating data), dplyr (transforming data), and ggplot2 (visualising data).

pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse)

p_load() from the pacman package is used to install (if not yet installed) and load the packages into R.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Importing Geospatial Data

Importing polygon feature data in shapefile format
st_read() is used to import MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL shapefile as a polygon feature data frame. The dsn argument specifies the data path and layer provides the shapefile name (no file extension needed).

mpsz = st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson") %>%

Attempting to overlay the preschool points on the mpsz layer:

text:
Working with Projection

Checking the coordinate system of a simple feature data frame
st_crs() is used to inspect the coordinate reference system of a sf object. Since mpsz was already transformed to svy21 during import, the EPSG code should be 3414:

st_crs(mpsz)

Coordinate Reference System:
  User input: EPSG:3414 
  wkt:
PROJCRS["SVY21 / Singapore TM",
    BASEGEOGCRS["SVY21",
        DATUM["SVY21",
            ELLIPSOID["WGS 84",6378137,298.257223563,
                LENGTHUNIT["metre",1]]],
        PRIMEM["Greenwich",0,
            ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
        ID["EPSG",4757]],
    CONVERSION["Singapore Transverse Mercator",
        METHOD["Transverse Mercator",
            ID["EPSG",9807]],
        PARAMETER["Latitude of natural origin",1.36666666666667,
            ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433],
            ID["EPSG",8801]],
        PARAMETER["Longitude of natural origin",103.833333333333,
            ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433],
            ID["EPSG",8802]],
        PARAMETER["Scale factor at natural origin",1,
            SCALEUNIT["unity",1],
            ID["EPSG",8805]],
        PARAMETER["False easting",28001.642,
            LENGTHUNIT["metre",1],
            ID["EPSG",8806]],
        PARAMETER["False northing",38744.572,
            LENGTHUNIT["metre",1],
            ID["EPSG",8807]]],
    CS[Cartesian,2],
        AXIS["northing (N)",north,
            ORDER[1],
            LENGTHUNIT["metre",1]],
        AXIS["easting (E)",east,
            ORDER[2],
            LENGTHUNIT["metre",1]],
    USAGE[
        SCOPE["Cadastre, engineering survey, topographic mapping."],
        AREA["Singapore - onshore and offshore."],
        BBOX[1.13,103.59,1.47,104.07]],
    ID["EPSG",3414]]


The output confirms mpsz is in svy21 (EPSG: 3414).






Note



In some workflows — particularly when importing shapefiles that were incorrectly labelled — the EPSG code may show as 9001 instead of 3414. In that case, st_set_crs(mpsz, 3414) can be used to assign the correct label. However, this only changes the label and does not mathematically reproject the coordinates. If the data is truly in WGS84 (as with GeoJSON files from data.gov.sg), st_transform(crs = 3414) must be used instead.




Transforming the projection of preschool from wgs84 to svy21
st_set_crs() only reassigns the label without mathematically reprojecting the coordinates. To actually reproject data from one CRS to another, st_transform() must be used:

preschool <- st_transform(preschool, crs = 3414)

plot(st_geometry(preschool), add = TRUE)








The composite map now displays as expected.

text:
Geoprocessing with sf package

Use case 1: Land acquisition analysis

The scenario
The authority plans to upgrade existing cycling paths and needs to acquire 5 metres of reserved land on both sides of each path. The task is to determine the extent and total area of land to be acquired.


The solution
First, st_buffer() is used to compute 5-metre buffers around cycling paths. The cycling path data is first transformed to svy21:

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)

Calculating the area of each buffer using the tidyverse approach:

buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))

Total land area to be acquired:

sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

3687875 [m^2]


To visualise the buffer within a specific planning subzone (Tampines West), filter() is used to extract the subzone polygon, followed by st_intersection() to clip the buffers:

mpsz_selected <- mpsz %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")


buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected)













Use case 2: Number of pre-schools by planning subzone

The scenario
The authority requires a count of pre-schools in each planning subzone to support forward planning.


The solution
st_intersects() identifies which pre-schools fall within each planning subzone, and lengths() counts them:

mpsz$`PreSch Count` <- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool))

Summary statistics of the new field:

Plotting the distribution of pre-school density using ggplot2:

title: In-class Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Lesson 1 covers geospatial data models, coordinate systems, and thematic mapping with tmap. The import, projection, and basic choropleth workflow were already practised in Hands-on Exercise 1a and 1b, so this in-class exercise focuses only on what is new:

title: In-class Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Geospatial Data Wrangling

Point-in-polygon count
st_intersects() returns, for each of the 332 planning subzones, the indices of the pre-schools falling inside it. lengths() collapses that list of index vectors into a single count per subzone:

mpsz19 <- mpsz19 %>%
  mutate(`PreSch Count` = lengths(
    st_intersects(mpsz19, preschool)))



Computing density
A raw count is not comparable across subzones of different size, so it is normalised by area. st_area() supplies the area, units::drop_units() strips the m^2 label so the result is a plain numeric, and multiplying by 1,000,000 converts the density to pre-schools per square kilometre:

mpsz19 <- mpsz19 %>%
  mutate(Area = units::drop_units(
    st_area(.)),
    `PreSch Density` = `PreSch Count` / Area * 1000000)







Note



Dropping the unit early matters. If left in place, the units label propagates through the arithmetic and ggstatsplot — which expects plain numeric vectors — fails on the column in the next section.



mpsz19 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  slice_max(`PreSch Count`, n = 5) %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, `PreSch Count`, `PreSch Density`)

title: In-class Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Statistical Analysis
The hands-on exercise plotted count against density with geom_point() and described the pattern by eye. Here the same relationship is examined with EDA and Confirmatory Data Analysis (CDA) together.
Geometry is dropped first, because ggscatterstats() expects an ordinary data frame:

mpsz19_df <- mpsz19 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(`PreSch Density` = as.numeric(`PreSch Density`),
         `PreSch Count` = as.numeric(`PreSch Count`))

ggscatterstats() draws the scatterplot, the marginal distributions, the fitted line, and the result of a parametric correlation test in one call:

ggscatterstats(data = mpsz19_df,
               x = `PreSch Density`,
               y = `PreSch Count`,
               type = "parametric",
               label.var = SUBZONE_N,
               label.expression = `PreSch Count` > 40)














NoteInterpretation



The subtitle reports the Pearson correlation together with its confidence interval, p-value, and sample size, which turns the visual impression into a testable claim: r = 0.64, 95% CI [0.57, 0.70], p < 0.001, n = 332.
So the relationship is positive and clearly significant, but only moderate — density explains roughly 40% of the variance in count. That gap is the substantive finding, not noise: a large outlying subzone can hold many pre-schools while remaining sparse, and a small dense residential subzone can reach a high density on only a handful. Count and density are therefore not interchangeable, and the choice between them changes what a choropleth map of pre-school provision would show. The labelled points are the subzones with more than 40 pre-schools.

title: In-class Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Preparing the Dependency Ratio
The analytical maps below need a continuous variable with a skewed distribution. The dependency ratio prepared in Hands-on Exercise 1b is reused, so the wrangling is repeated here only in condensed form:

popdata2024 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv") %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG, values_from = POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(select(., `0_to_4`, `5_to_9`, `10_to_14`,
                                   `15_to_19`, `20_to_24`), na.rm = TRUE),
         `ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(select(., `25_to_29`, `30_to_34`,
                                              `35_to_39`, `40_to_44`,
                                              `45_to_49`, `50_to_54`,
                                              `55_to_59`, `60_to_64`), na.rm = TRUE),
         `AGED` = rowSums(select(., `65_to_69`, `70_to_74`, `75_to_79`,
                                    `80_to_84`, `85_to_89`, `90_and_over`), na.rm = TRUE),
         `TOTAL` = rowSums(select(., `0_to_4`:`90_and_over`), na.rm = TRUE),
         `DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`) %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ), .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)







Warning



pivot_wider() orders the new columns alphabetically, placing 5_to_9 after 55_to_59. Selecting age groups by position (rowSums(.[3:6])) therefore assigns the wrong bands to YOUNG and ECONOMY ACTIVE. The columns are referenced by name above so the derivation is independent of column order.


Joining with the geospatial layer as the left table keeps the geometry column, so the result remains an sf object. Rows with missing values are dropped, because the break points below are computed with quantile(), which cannot work over NA:

mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz19, popdata2024,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ")) %>%
  drop_na()

write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")

title: In-class Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Analytical Map: Percentile Map
The classification methods available through style in tm_scale_intervals() all place the breaks for you. An analytical map instead computes its own breaks, so that the classes carry a specific statistical meaning.
A percentile map is a quantile map with six fixed categories — 0–1%, 1–10%, 10–50%, 50–90%, 90–99%, 99–100% — obtained by passing an explicit vector of cumulative probabilities to quantile(). Both endpoints must be included.

The get.var() function
Extracts a variable from an sf data frame as a plain, unnamed vector.

arguments — vname: variable name as a quoted character; df: an sf data frame
returns — a vector of values with no column name


get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>%
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}



The percentmap() function

percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle = NA, mtitle = "Percentile Map") {

  # cumulative probabilities defining the six percentile classes
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)

  # extract the variable and derive its percentile break points
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent)

  if (is.na(legtitle)) legtitle <- vnam

  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam,
            fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              breaks = bperc,
              values = "brewer.blues",
              labels = c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%",
                         "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%")),
            fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legtitle)) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_title(mtitle)
}







Notetmap v4 syntax



Lesson 1 and the earlier cohorts’ exercises use tmap v3, where breaks, palette, and labels are passed straight to tm_fill(). In tmap 4.x they belong to a scale specification handed to fill.scale, the legend title moves into tm_legend() via fill.legend, and the map title becomes a standalone tm_title() element instead of tm_layout(main.title =).

packageVersion("tmap")

[1] '4.2'





percentmap("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2024,
           legtitle = "Dependency ratio",
           mtitle = "Percentile Map of Dependency Ratio")








The percentile map isolates the extremes a standard quantile map hides: the outer classes hold only the top and bottom 1% of subzones, so genuinely unusual values stand out instead of being absorbed into a broad top class.

title: In-class Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Analytical Map: Box Map
A box map is an augmented quartile map with two extra classes for outliers, using the fences of a boxplot as break points. Which value opens the sequence depends on whether outliers exist:

no lower outliers — the first break is the lower fence and the second is the minimum, so the first class is necessarily empty;
lower outliers present — the first break is the minimum and the second is the lower fence.

The upper end follows the same logic in reverse.

The boxbreaks() function

arguments — v: vector of observations; mult: multiplier for the IQR, default 1.5
returns — a vector of seven break points


boxbreaks <- function(v, mult = 1.5) {

  qv <- unname(quantile(v))

  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr

  # seven break points define the six box map classes
  bb <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = 7)

  if (lofence < qv[1]) {   # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {                 # lower outliers present
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
    bb[2] <- lofence
  }

  if (upfence > qv[5]) {   # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {                 # upper outliers present
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }

  # Q1, median and Q3 form the three interior breaks
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]

  return(bb)
}

The breaks produced for the dependency ratio:

boxbreaks(get.var("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2024))

[1]  0.0000000  0.4666279  0.6750233  0.7283114  0.8139535  1.0223488 10.0000000




The boxmap() function

arguments — vnam: variable name as a quoted character; df: an sf polygon layer; legtitle: legend title; mtitle: map title; mult: IQR multiplier
returns — a tmap element that plots the map


boxmap <- function(vnam, df,
                   legtitle = NA,
                   mtitle = "Box Map",
                   mult = 1.5) {

  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var, mult)

  if (is.na(legtitle)) legtitle <- vnam

  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam,
            fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              breaks = bb,
              values = "brewer.blues",
              labels = c("Lower outlier",
                         "< 25%",
                         "25% - 50%",
                         "50% - 75%",
                         "> 75%",
                         "Upper outlier")),
            fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legtitle)) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_title(mtitle)
}



Static box map

boxmap("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2024,
       legtitle = "Dependency ratio",
       mtitle = "Box Map of Dependency Ratio")














NoteInterpretation



The two outlier classes are what distinguish a box map from an ordinary quartile map, and both are populated here — 17 subzones fall below the lower fence of 0.467 and 3 above the upper fence of 1.022.
The lower outliers are almost entirely city-centre subzones — Clarke Quay, City Hall, Boat Quay, Tanjong Pagar, Cecil — where the resident population is small and overwhelmingly working-age. The upper outliers are the opposite case, and Loyang West is the extreme: 500 aged residents against only 50 economy active, giving a dependency ratio of 10 against a median of 0.73.
That single value is worth pausing on. It stretches the top class from 1.02 all the way to 10, which is exactly why the box map is the right tool here: an ordinary quartile map would have buried it in a “> 75%” class alongside subzones with a ratio of 0.9, whereas the box map flags it as statistically exceptional and prompts the follow-up question.








WarningSmall denominators



SingStat rounds subzone populations to the nearest 10, so a ratio computed over a denominator of 50 residents is highly unstable — one rounding step moves it substantially. The most extreme values at both ends of this map sit in subzones with fewer than a few hundred residents, so they are better read as a signal to check the underlying counts than as a reliable measure of demographic structure.




Interactive box map
tmap_mode("view") switches to interactive rendering, and tm_basemap() places a reference tile layer underneath so the outlier subzones can be located on the ground. (The v3 guard tmap_options(check.and.fix = TRUE) is not needed — that option no longer exists in tmap 4.x, which validates geometries on its own.)

tmap_mode("view")

tm_basemap("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas") +
boxmap("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2024,
       legtitle = "Dependency ratio")







tmap_mode("plot")

tmap_mode() is a global setting, so it is reset to "plot" immediately afterwards to keep later chunks static.
